rationale: A wins because it does the adult work: it turns a thin seed-round update into four genuinely different reporter-shaped paths, then tells the founder which ones collapse without proof. Its best line, "Verdano's three utility pilots are the story its funding round isn't," finds the real trade angle and names the missing evidence. B has usable instincts, but "Local grids are straining under community solar growth" smuggles in a market trend the update never gave us, and the contrarian solar framing leans on borrowed drama.
gaps_in_A: "Ex-Tesla Energy and NREL engineers are betting community solar breaks the grid before rooftop does" invents a rooftop-vs-community-solar comparison the update does not support.
"the community-solar bottleneck is software, not panels" is a sharp thesis, but still overstates the supplied facts unless third-party evidence appears.
The founder angle asks for roles and IP correctly, but the headline should not imply a technical lineage from Tesla/NREL before those details are verified.
gaps_in_B: "community solar growth" is not in the update. No market-growth data was supplied, so the trend angle starts with an unsupported premise.
"An ex-Tesla Energy engineer and an ex-NREL researcher" invents job functions. The update only says ex-Tesla Energy and ex-NREL founders.
"neither prior employer solved outright" is invented color. It sounds smart and creates a fact-check trap.
B refuses the customer-story route as a "duplicate," but that is probably the most journalistically useful angle if one utility will go on record.
